section_summary: This section documents the severe political crisis in Japan precipitated by the assassination of Prime Minister Tsuyoshi Inukai during the May 15 Incident of 1932 and its international repercussions. It contains extensive diplomatic despatches, cross-reference sheets, and telegrams detailing Japanese ultra-nationalist societies, bitter disputes between the Seiyukai Cabinet and the military over the South Manchuria Railway, and growing domestic agitation favoring withdrawal from the League of Nations. Despatches from Tokyo, Peiping, Shanghai, and Washington chronicle the collapse of party government, Chinese and Soviet anxieties over Japanese military expansion, and the eventual installation of a transitional national coalition ministry under Admiral Viscount Makoto Saito.

subfiles.about: Roster and analytical profiles of Japanese nationalist, reactionary, patriotic, and state-socialist organizations transmitted as enclosures to Despatch No. 588.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: This document comprises two detailed enclosures to Tokyo Despatch No. 588 surveying reactionary and nationalist societies in Japan. The first part concludes an extensive numerical catalogue (entries 55 through 124) listing organization names, English translations, founding dates, headquarters, leaders, publications, and memberships. The second enclosure provides comprehensive profiles of seven leading reactionary bodies: Dai Nippon Kokusui-kai, Dai Nippon Seigi-dan, Dai Nippon Seisan-to, Kenkoku-kai, Kokuryu-kai (Black Dragon Society), Nippon Shakai-Shugi Kenkyu-jo, and Zen-Nippon Aikokusha Kyodotoso Kyogikai. The report emphasizes the groups' monarchist tenets, anti-communist agitation, rejection of parliamentary capitalism, advocacy of state socialism, and growing sympathy among junior army and naval officers.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 588: Reactionary and Nationalist Organizations in Japan (Enclosures)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording Despatch No. 586 concerning the dismissal of South Manchuria Railway Vice President Eguchi.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Despatch No. 586 (893.22/2857): the Japanese Government's dismissal of South Manchuria Railway Vice President Eguchi and the public reaction.
subfiles.title: Document File Note regarding South Manchuria Railway Vice President Eguchi Dismissal (Despatch No. 586)

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting on the dismissal of South Manchuria Railway Vice President Teijo Eguchi, Count Uchida's resignation, and the resulting clash between the Seiyukai Cabinet and the military.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 586 reports that the Seiyukai Cabinet obtained an Imperial ordinance dismissing Teijo Eguchi as Vice President of the South Manchuria Railway, prompting Railway President Count Yasuya Uchida and several directors to submit their resignations. The action drew fierce public and editorial condemnation against the Inukai administration for subordinating national interests in Manchuria to partisan spoils. Japanese military authorities in Kwantung and War Minister Sadao Araki strongly objected to party interference and blocked the appointment of Seiyukai politician Jotaro Yamamoto, insisting that railway management cooperate strictly with military policy. The despatch includes a translated editorial from the Hochi Shimbun entitled 'Tyranny of Seiyukai,' which excoriates the government's despotic methods and partisan corruption.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 586: Dismissal of Vice President Eguchi of the South Manchuria Railway

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording Despatch No. 590 concerning Cabinet approval of a supplementary budget for peace preservation expenditures.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Despatch No. 590 (894.51/357): the Cabinet approved a supplementary budget with peace preservation funds after recent assassinations.
subfiles.title: Document File Note regarding Supplementary Budget for Peace Preservation (Despatch No. 590)

subfiles.about: Urgent telegram reporting the shooting of Prime Minister Tsuyoshi Inukai, attacks on Count Makino's residence, and bombings across Tokyo during the May 15 Incident.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Reports Prime Minister Inukai was shot and critically wounded on May 15, 1932, by attackers in military uniform who also hit Makino's residence, police headquarters and Seiyukai headquarters. Tokyo is otherwise quiet; no danger to Americans.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 126 from Tokyo reporting the Assassination of Prime Minister Inukai (May 15 Incident)

subfiles.about: Telegraphic instruction to the American Embassy in Tokyo to express condolences on the shooting of Prime Minister Inukai.
subfiles.from: William R. Castle Jr. (Acting Secretary of State), Department of State, Washington
subfiles.summary: State Department instructs the Tokyo Embassy to convey official condolences on the attack on Prime Minister Inukai.
subfiles.title: Telegram from State Department to Tokyo Expressing Condolences on Prime Minister Inukai's Death

subfiles.about: Telegram confirming execution of condolence instructions and reporting the collective resignation of the Japanese Cabinet.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Neville reports condolences delivered; the Cabinet has resigned, and it is too early to judge political developments.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 128 from Tokyo regarding Cabinet Resignation following Inukai Assassination

subfiles.about: Telegram from former Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes requesting the State Department to cable personal condolences to Foreign Minister Yoshizawa.
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, Boston, Massachusetts
subfiles.summary: Former Ambassador Forbes asks the Department to cable Neville, at his own expense, his personal regret to Yoshizawa over Inukai's assassination.
subfiles.title: Telegram from W. Cameron Forbes to State Department Requesting Message of Regret to Yoshizawa

subfiles.about: Instruction relaying former Ambassador Forbes's personal message of sympathy to Japanese Foreign Minister Kenkichi Yoshizawa.
subfiles.from: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State, Washington
subfiles.summary: Stimson relays former Ambassador Forbes's message of regret over Inukai's assassination to the Tokyo Embassy for delivery to Yoshizawa.
subfiles.title: Telegram from State Department to Tokyo Relaying Forbes's Message to Yoshizawa

subfiles.about: Report on post-assassination political negotiations, Genro Saionji's summons to Tokyo, and military opposition to party government.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Neville reports no new government yet; Prince Saionji summoned to advise on a premier. Army officers refuse to cooperate with party government; Takahashi is provisional Prime Minister.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 132 from Tokyo on Political Crisis and Formation of New Government

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording Despatch No. 560 explaining Home Minister Nakahashi's resignation over the Sakuradamon Incident.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Despatch No. 560 (894.00 P.R./52): Home Minister Nakahashi's resignation was a delayed consequence of the January 1932 attempt on the Emperor.
subfiles.title: Document File Note regarding Resignation of Home Minister Nakahashi (Despatch No. 560)

subfiles.about: Telegram quoting a Moscow broadcast by the Red Army Chief of Staff analyzing Inukai's murder and Soviet-Japanese relations.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Quotes a Moscow dispatch on a Red Army Chief of Staff's radio address linking Inukai's killing to anti-Soviet hostility. He says understanding with the Japanese military is impossible.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 541 from Peiping Quoting Soviet Reaction to Inukai's Assassination

subfiles.about: Extensive compilation of Chinese vernacular and foreign press commentary on the assassination of Premier Inukai and the rise of Japanese fascism.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Telegram No. 548 transmits comprehensive extracts of Chinese and foreign editorial opinion across Shanghai, Peiping, Tientsin, Canton, and Nanking regarding Inukai's assassination. Major newspapers including China Times, Shun Pao, Sin Wan Pao, North China Daily News, China Press, Ta Kung Pao, and Central Daily News interpreted the outrage as a fascist military coup aimed at overthrowing parliamentary government, annexing Manchuria and Mongolia, and pursuing war with Soviet Russia and the United States. Commentators underscored the irony of Japan portraying China as an unorganized state when Tokyo could not protect its own Premier in his official residence. The press concluded that Inukai's removal foreshadows an aggressive military dictatorship and heightened military pressure on China.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 548 from Peiping Relaying Chinese and Foreign Press Reactions to Inukai's Assassination

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording Telegram No. 549 regarding Wang Ching-wei's concerns over the establishment of a military government in Japan.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Peiping Telegram No. 549 (793.94/5241): Wang Ching-wei fears a Japanese military regime after Inukai's assassination would worsen relations.
subfiles.title: Document File Note regarding Wang Ching-wei's Fears of Japanese Military Government (Telegram No. 549)

subfiles.about: Telegram transmitting Kuo Wen report of an interview with Executive Yuan President Wang Ching-wei on talks with Akira Ariyoshi and domestic political reform.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Relays Wang Ching-wei's interview on his talk with Akira Ariyoshi: Chinese boycott will end only if Japan reverses policy. He says a Japanese military government would worsen matters.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 549 from Peiping reporting Wang Ching-wei's Press Interview on Inukai's Death and Ariyoshi's Visit

subfiles.about: Report quoting Nippon Dempo on younger Japanese army officers' uncompromising rejection of party government and their thirteen demands.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Relays a press report that young officers reject any party cabinet; Araki and Masaki cannot restrain them, making a Suzuki Seiyukai cabinet doubtful. Junior officers presented thirteen demands.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 553 from Peiping reporting Military Demands and Opposition to Party Government

subfiles.about: Confidential report on rumors linking officer suicides and battlefield deaths in China to the October 1931 coup and Blood Brotherhood assassinations.
subfiles.from: Erle R. Dickover, American Consul, Kobe
subfiles.summary: Consul Dickover reports a rumor that officers implicated in the October 1931 coup were sent to China to die, and that one supplied the guns used by the Blood Brotherhood.
subfiles.title: Letter from Consul Dickover to Neville regarding Rumors on Officer Suicides and Blood Brotherhood Assassinations
subfiles.to: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo

subfiles.about: Official record of discussion between Secretary Stimson and Ambassador Debuchi regarding condolences, cabinet reorganization, and Shanghai troop withdrawals.
subfiles.from: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State, Washington
subfiles.summary: Stimson tells Ambassador Debuchi gratitude for condolences is noted. Debuchi says the new government will not be fascist, and Japan will withdraw from Shanghai regardless; round table conference mentioned.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation between Secretary of State Stimson and Japanese Ambassador Debuchi

subfiles.about: Strictly confidential instruction transmitting to Chargé Neville a copy of Secretary Stimson's conversation with Ambassador Debuchi.
subfiles.from: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State, Washington
subfiles.summary: Instruction No. 322 sends Neville Stimson's May 19 memorandum of conversation with Debuchi, for his personal information and not for embassy staff.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 322 from Secretary Stimson to Neville Transmitting Debuchi Memorandum
subfiles.to: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo

subfiles.about: Strictly confidential instruction transmitting to Minister Johnson a copy of Secretary Stimson's conversation with Ambassador Debuchi.
subfiles.from: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State, Washington
subfiles.summary: Stimson sends Minister Johnson in Peiping his May 19 conversation with Debuchi; Johnson may show it to Legation Counselors.
subfiles.title: Instruction from Secretary Stimson to Johnson Transmitting Debuchi Memorandum
subfiles.to: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister, Peiping

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting that Admiral Viscount Makoto Saito received the Imperial command to form a compromise national cabinet.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Reports Admiral Viscount Saito received the Imperial command to form a cabinet on May 22, 1932. His selection as a compromise is widely welcomed despite regret at the end of party government.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 136 from Tokyo reporting Imperial Command to Admiral Saito to Form Cabinet

subfiles.about: Inquiry from Minister Johnson whether the State Department desires summaries of Tokyo press reports received in Peiping repeated via naval radio.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Johnson asks whether the Department wants press reports on Tokyo political developments repeated by naval radio at no expense.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 561 from Peiping Inquiring on Transmission of Tokyo Press Reports via Naval Radio

subfiles.about: State Department instruction requesting the Peiping Legation to transmit texts and summaries of Tokyo press reports via naval radio.
subfiles.from: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State, Washington
subfiles.summary: The Department tells Minister Johnson to send important Tokyo press reports on the Japanese political crisis by naval radio.
subfiles.title: Telegram from State Department to Peiping Requesting Tokyo Press Reports by Naval Radio

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting that rumors of the death of General Yoshinori Shirakawa in Shanghai are premature.
subfiles.from: Edwin S. Cunningham, American Consul General, Shanghai
subfiles.summary: The Japanese Consul General says rumors of General Shirakawa's death, after the Hongkew Park bombing, are premature.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 262 from Shanghai regarding False Rumor of General Shirakawa's Death

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording Despatch No. 611 concerning press agitation in Japan favoring withdrawal from the League of Nations.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Despatch No. 611 (793.94/5251): strong Japanese press and public sentiment for withdrawing from the League of Nations.
subfiles.title: Document File Note regarding Press Comment on Japan's Possible Withdrawal from the League of Nations (Despatch No. 611)

subfiles.about: Analysis of mounting Japanese agitation to withdraw from the League of Nations, featuring translations of press articles and a cautionary critique by Dr. Hitoshi Ashida.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 611 examines intense public and military agitation in Japan advocating secession from the League of Nations. Neville highlights militant speeches by War Minister Sadao Araki and editorial series in the Osaka Mainichi arguing that the League is an obstructive European body that fails to understand Far Eastern realities. The despatch includes two translated enclosures: an article outlining the economic perils and treaty complications of withdrawal, and a penetrating essay by former diplomat Dr. Hitoshi Ashida entitled 'Japan's Diplomacy at a Turning Point.' Ashida urges prudence, comparing Japan's current war fever to pre-war imperial Germany and warning that quitting the League would surrender Japan's permanent Council seat, forfeit mandatory authority over the South Sea Islands, and invite catastrophic international isolation.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 611: Press Comment regarding Possibility of Withdrawal by Japan from the League of Nations

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording Telegram No. 556 concerning Akira Ariyoshi's conversations with Wang Ching-wei and Lo Wen-kan.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Telegram No. 556 (793.94/5346): Ariyoshi spoke only in generalities with Wang Ching-wei and Lo Wen-kan and left on hearing of Inukai's assassination.
subfiles.title: Document File Note regarding Ariyoshi's Conversations with Wang Ching-wei and Lo Wen-kan (Telegram No. 556)

subfiles.about: Report transmitting Nanking findings that Akira Ariyoshi had acted as a direct personal emissary of the late Premier Inukai.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Nanking reports Ariyoshi came as Inukai's confidential emissary but, with Inukai assassinated that day, spoke only in generalities and left for Shanghai.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 556 from Peiping transmitting Nanking Report on Ariyoshi's Mission as Inukai's Emissary

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording Despatch No. 600 containing the Japan monthly political report for April 1932.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Despatch No. 600 (894.00 P.R./53): no prospect of political improvement, and the Seiyukai faced intense criticism in April 1932.
subfiles.title: Document File Note regarding General Political Situation and Criticisms of Seiyukai (Despatch No. 600)

subfiles.about: Embassy report extract detailing the deepening crisis of the Inukai Cabinet, economic distress, Minseito platform changes, and growing attraction to fascism.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: April 1932 political report: worsening economy and the Eguchi dismissal (Uchida resigned) brought condemnation of Inukai. The Minseito dropped the gold standard; fascism and unrest grew.
subfiles.title: Extract from Despatch No. 600: Political Report for April 1932 (General Political Situation and Opposition Activities)

subfiles.about: Report on the formal installation of Viscount Saito's national coalition cabinet and plans to convene an extraordinary Diet session.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Reports the Saito Cabinet was installed May 26, 1932, with Saito also holding Foreign Affairs. It includes both major parties and non-partisans; the Diet will take up relief plans.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 141 from Tokyo reporting Installation of the Saito Cabinet

subfiles.about: Transmission of Japanese press reports detailing the ministerial roster of the Saito Cabinet and initial reactions from political, financial, and military circles.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Relays the full Saito cabinet line-up from Nippon Dempo. Public and business are disappointed by second-tier appointees; party friction is expected, and the military sees it as transitional.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 571 from Peiping transmitting Nippon Dempo Reports on Saito Cabinet Line-up and Public Reception

subfiles.about: Transmission of a Reuter dispatch from Tokyo detailing administrative reshuffles, military promotions, and party alignments under the Saito Cabinet.
subfiles.from: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Relays a Reuter dispatch on appointments under Saito, including Kodama as Formosa governor and Kawashima in Korea. Public relief at the crisis's end; Uchida may yet take Foreign Affairs.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 572 from Peiping transmitting Reuter Report on Military and Administrative Appointments under Saito Cabinet
